title: Julie Ann McIlwaine: Murder conviction overturned for woman who killed abusive partner
description: A west Belfast woman who stabbed her abusive partner to death while he slept has had her conviction for murder overturned.The Court of Appeal ruled th
body: A west Belfast woman who stabbed her abusive partner to death while he slept has had her conviction for murder overturned.The Court of Appeal ruled that jurors were misdirected on Julie Ann McIlwaine's loss of control defence to the killing of James Joseph Crossley in March 2022.Senior judges quashed the guilty verdict and gave the prosecution two weeks to decide if it is to seek any retrial."We cannot be satisfied that the conviction is safe," said Lady Chief Justice Dame Siobhan Keegan.McIlwaine, 35, who has been serving a minimum 12-year jail term, wept on the videolink from Hydebank Prison as the ruling was delivered.She admitted killing her partner but denied murder, claiming to have suffered a temporary loss of control as a victim of domestic abuse.Crossley, 38, was stabbed up to 10 times in the chest and abdomen as he lay sleeping beside the couple's young child at McIlwaine's former home in Dunmurry.The pair had been in a relationship marred by emotional manipulation and coercive control.At the time of his death, Crossley was on bail for an alleged assault against McIlwaine and subject to a restraining order prohibiting any contact with her.Despite a period of separation, they had re-established their relationship by the night of the killing.The court heard Crossley took medication and went to sleep after arguments in which he issued an ultimatum for McIlwaine to choose between him and her family.During police interviews McIlwaine stated that she had considered taking her own life.She described taking a knife from the kitchen, returning to the bedroom and moving the child before repeatedly stabbing her sleeping partner.Prosecutors argued that she made rational choices which demonstrated being in control of her actions.In October 2024, a jury rejected McIlwaine's case and unanimously found her guilty of murder.Defence lawyers argued on appeal that they had been misdirected and reached a verdict which went against the weight of expert evidence.Central to the appeal was how the trial judge advised jurors on the legal test for the loss-of-control defence.Instead of asking them to decide if someone of similar characteristics to McIlwaine "might" have reacted similarly, the question posed was "would" that person have acted in the same way.Dame Siobhan, sitting with Lord Justice Colton, backed defence submissions that the wording used wrongly imposed a higher threshold for establishing probability.Two consultant forensic psychiatrists had also concluded that a properly directed jury could find McIlwaine met the criteria necessary to establish loss of self-control.Both witnesses highlighted the psychological impact of prolonged abuse and the recognised behaviour responses of victims in coercively controlling relationships."The misdirection we have identified was highly material, given the uncontradicted expert evidence," said the Lady Chief Justice."The appeal succeeds… and the conviction for murder will accordingly be quashed."Adjourning the case until 16 October, she told prosecution counsel: "You have to come back to court on what steps you want to take."

schema.headline: Julie Ann McIlwaine: Murder conviction overturned for woman who killed abusive partner

title: Conservatives aim to be election-ready ahead of party conference
description: When Kemi Badenoch arrived for her first Conservative conference as leader last year, a member of her entourage overheard somebody wonder aloud: "Who'
body: When Kemi Badenoch arrived for her first Conservative conference as leader last year, a member of her entourage overheard somebody wonder aloud: "Who's that?"This baffled member of the public was actually working at the Conservative conference. Badenoch had been the party's leader and the leader of the opposition for almost a year.It is an anecdote which underlines the scale of the challenge Badenoch faced at that conference, an event her allies are now with distance willing to acknowledge was make or break for her leadership.And it is an anecdote which also underlines that, far from break her, that conference represented the start of a major turnaround for Badenoch.Twelve months on, Badenoch will arrive in Birmingham this weekend in total command of a party whose leading lights are beginning to permit themselves the occasional flicker of optimism after years of misery preparing for, and then experiencing, a brutal election defeat.Yet for all that Conservatives now believe their leader is an electoral asset, they still face an existential threat from Reform UK and the challenge of how to adjust their strategy to face a new prime minister, Andy Burnham.The answer to both those issues for Badenoch is a focus on the economy. "Stronger economy, stronger country" will be the party's conference slogan, with the two speeches Badenoch gives - one on Sunday, the other on Wednesday - building on announcements she has made in the past two weeks about cutting benefits for the long-term unemployed.Welfare spending is increasingly seen by the Conservatives as a core battleground with Labour.During Labour conference they derided the event as the "Welfare Party Conference". Whereas Sir Keir Starmer sought to cut welfare spending before backing down in the face of a rebellion by his own MPs, Burnham has made clear that he believes the way to reduce the benefits bill in the long-term is more up-front investment in support for those out of work.This is a clear ideological difference which both parties are happy to embrace. Conservative strategists believe there is a broader lesson there. "The differences between the parties have been quite muddled for a while," one says. "Now that Burnham is prime minister we have a more traditional left-right split."Another area where Badenoch will embrace that divide in the coming days is the pensions triple-lock.The policy currently guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% – whichever is the highest.Badenoch will make clear that the Conservatives continue to support that policy in its current form, breaking with some generally supportive think tanks and policy experts who believe Badenoch should follow Burnham's lead.In his conference speech on Tuesday, Burnham set out plans to end the existing triple lock from 2030, so the state pension increases at least by inflation or 2.5% - but remove the automatic annual link with average earnings.The Conservatives hope the sharpening left-right split leaves Reform UK in a strategic bind, occupying a less obvious place on that spectrum. A year ago some senior Conservatives feared being usurped by Reform as the leading party of the right was a near-inevitability, but now they are optimistic that Nigel Farage's party is on an inexorable slide.That bullishness is fuelled in large part by the difficulties Reform has faced over Nigel Farage's £5m gift from Christopher Harborne and the fallout - including a police inquiry - from the recent Channel 4 News investigation."I find more and more voters raise concerns about Reform with me - people who weren't previously giving us the time of day," one MP said. "These are successful people with big garages and good jobs who do not necessarily pay that much attention but want a small-c conservative government."They were switching to Reform because they were fed up with us and thought Farage was now the main option on the right. But they are starting to come back."Others are less positive, pointing out that Reform still often record higher shares than the Conservatives in the polls  — and more importantly have now won far more votes than them in successive years of local and national elections.Whether or not there is indeed a long-term trend of the Conservatives regaining ground at Reform's expense, Badenoch may not have long enough to wait. She has told her team to prepare for this conference as if it is the last before the general election. While not all of her aides agree, Badenoch is convinced that Burnham will go to the polls within the next year.Party high command started weekly election planning meetings shortly after Burnham succeeded Starmer. Neil O'Brien, a member of Badenoch's shadow cabinet, has begun work on a manifesto alongside the party's head of policy. It is intended to be a more concise set of pledges than the usual sprawling manifestos.Also with an eye to the election, the Conservatives will present new faces at the conference who have applied to be candidates at the next election. Badenoch's ambivalence in some cases, and opposition in others, to ex-MPs who lost their seats in 2024 standing for the party again has attracted some controversy, especially when it comes to the high-profile former cabinet ministers Grant Shapps and Penny Mordaunt.The leader's supporters are unrepentant, arguing that the party "needs to show we have changed".Things have certainly changed since last year, at least. That may prove the easy part.

schema.headline: Conservatives aim to be election-ready ahead of party conference

title: Thomas Tuchel: England boss would 'never rule out' selecting players in lower divisions
description: England are preparing to play Croatia in the Nations League in Rijeka on Saturday (17:00 BST).Speaking to the media on Friday, Tuchel said the City ve
body: England are preparing to play Croatia in the Nations League in Rijeka on Saturday (17:00 BST).Speaking to the media on Friday, Tuchel said the City verdict was a "big subject" in the England camp.Asked if he would select players not playing in the top flight, the manager said: "There is always a possibility."I would always try to pick the best team for the camp, for the occasion, for the tournament. "I will never rule out that because they don't play in the top flight in their country. We need to look at it case by case."All 24 players in the current England squad play in top leagues for their clubs and it is very unusual for a player to represent the Three Lions if they are not in a top division. However, James Trafford was in Tuchel squads in March and June 2025 while still in the Championship with Burnley, but he was an unused substitute on those occasions and did not win a full cap until he returned to Manchester City. Goalkeeper Sam Johnstone was the last player to represent England while playing in the Championship, for West Brom in 2021, while Kalvin Phillips - then at Leeds - made his debut for England before he had played in the Premier League. Asked about his players discussing the City verdict, Tuchel said: "We had some time off between the matches and it is a big subject. Everyone speaks about it, so there is no other voice needed"I am glad to be not that voice. No-one needs my half knowledge on the topic."Of course, the players talk about it. City players talk about it. We talk with them but only briefly. "They are ready to go tomorrow, that's what they show on the pitch and in camp. But of course, it's a big topic in the camp."

schema.headline: Thomas Tuchel: England boss would 'never rule out' selecting players in lower divisions

title: Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France
description: On Friday, a 17-year-old was arrested on suspicion of attempted homicide after protests in Belfort, north-eastern France, where a police officer was t
body: On Friday, a 17-year-old was arrested on suspicion of attempted homicide after protests in Belfort, north-eastern France, where a police officer was targeted.At least 65 staff members have been injured in the unrest, the education ministry said.In the Paris suburb of Pantin police charged at protesters and made arrests after projectiles where thrown at officers.Meanwhile, in Strasbourg tear gas was deployed as police feared conditions would become more hostile, according to the Reuters news agency.Rubbish bins have also been set on fire in Rennes and Paris."As far as we're concerned, we've won - our school is closed this morning," Lola, a 16-year-old protester, told the AFP news agency on Friday.She said police actions had made things worse."It makes us even angrier - the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us," she added.Police published pictures of some of the items they had seized from demonstrators, including petrol bombs, an axe and so-called mortar fireworks. "Significant damage" had been done to school facilities, the education ministry said, after attacks on school gates, entrances and fences.Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes suffered more than €2m (£1.7m) damage, according to the regional government, after fire destroyed its glass entrance and some areas inside the school.

schema.headline: Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France

title: Bahrain GP in Malaysia 2026: Russell says Red Bull strongest
description: Red Bull were tipped by George Russell and Charles Leclerc as the team to beat after the first day at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.Red Bull driv
body: Red Bull were tipped by George Russell and Charles Leclerc as the team to beat after the first day at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.Red Bull drivers Isack Hadjar and Max Verstappen finished the day second and fourth fastest but those positions appeared to belie their underlying pace.Ferrari's Leclerc was fastest by 0.099 seconds from Hadjar, while Verstappen was 0.257secs off the pace and behind McLaren's Lando Norris.Lewis Hamilton was fifth fastest and 0.305secs off the pace in the second Ferrari.But Verstappen did not do a qualifying simulation run on the soft tyre, and Leclerc said Hadjar had not optimised his.Leclerc said: "Everybody is very close. It's been a very difficult day overall."The track conditions were very tricky. The track was quite dirty and very slippery so things will evolve and change a lot from today until tomorrow and we have to be on the good side of that anticipating that in the best possible way."I felt quite good with the car but I still feel like the Red Bull is standing out this weekend so far."Isack did some mistakes in the last part of the lap and Max didn't do the lap on the soft tyres."I don't think we are the most competitive and also the Mercedes is a bit difficult to understand. I'm sure once Mercedes put everything together they will be very strong. Normally when they put something on the car it works."Verstappen, who chose not to do a soft-tyre run because rain was forecast and he wanted to prioritise race preparation, said his day had been a "decent start" and "positive".Technical director Pierre Wache added: "We were not very optimistic starting the weekend. The main aspect was to evaluate the package we put in Baku in different type of corners than low speed."It looks to be working better than the previous package. Relative performance is difficult to judge but we were surprisingly happy with where we were today."Mercedes drivers Russell and Kimi Antonelli were only seventh and eighth fastest in terms of headline times as they evaluated a major upgrade on their car, the team's first since the Canadian Grand Prix in June.Russell said: "I'm feeling the downforce in some of the corners but with this amount of tyre overheating and degradation that trumps everything. So we just need to get on top of that overnight,. That's more of a set-up rather than the upgrade itself and go from there.'Asked whether he could compete for pole position on Saturday, Russell said: "Currently, Verstappen looks very fast and the race pace of the McLaren looked very quick but never say never."The Briton trails Antonelli by 66 points in the championship after his victory in Azerbaijan last weekend.On the race simulation runs, Verstappen also looked like the car to beat, taking stint length and tyre wear into account.But the top four teams all looked to be in close company after a day evaluating tyre wear in the tropical temperatures and on an abnormally abrasive track, where F1 cars last raced in 2017.Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and Alpine's Pierre Gasly were ninth and 10th.Three drivers have grid penalties. Hadjar will drop five places from his qualifying position for exceeding the permitted number of engine parts.And Arvid Lindblad of Racing Bulls and Alpine's Franco Colapinto will be at the back, the Briton for engine penalties, and the Argentine because of a 10-place engine penalty on top of the five-place penalty he was given for causing a crash at a restart in last weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix.F1 has returned to this track, regarded as one of the best layouts among the new generation of circuits that came on stream at the end of the last century and into this one, because of the circumstances around this year's calendar.The Bahrain and Saudi Arabia races were cancelled at the beginning of the year as a result of the war in the Middle East.But Bahrain were keen to hold their race and Crown Prince Salman bin Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa negotiated to hold the race in Malaysia.A bunch of Bahraini-related activities are being held at the track, while the trophy presented will be the Bahrain Grand Prix trophy and rosewater rather than champagne will be sprayed on the podium.

schema.headline: Bahrain GP in Malaysia 2026: Russell says Red Bull strongest

title: Intensified Russian strikes are tearing Kyiv apart, Klitschko warns
description: "We're talking about survival," Klitschko said at Friday's defence council meeting with Kyiv's top military, security, emergencies and police official
body: "We're talking about survival," Klitschko said at Friday's defence council meeting with Kyiv's top military, security, emergencies and police officials.Russia's aim was to "sow panic", he said, stressing that the capital would "prevail - but only through the joint efforts of those who love it and care for it".The mayor was speaking just hours after Kyiv's key Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was hit in an overnight Russian drone attack. On Friday evening it was struck again - the fourth time in two days.The bridge is one of the main transport arteries across the Dnipro River dividing western and eastern parts of Kyiv.All metro and automobile traffic is now suspended across the bridge, causing major delays across the city. Restrictions are also in place on Kyiv's two other key bridges.Kyiv's current population is estimated to be about three million, and many residents rely heavily on the city's metro network. One person was killed in the capital when a multi-storey residential building was hit overnight, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Putin had decided in early September that "there are no rules now" when attacking Ukraine.In a published excerpt from his interview to the Financial Times, Zelensky said: "The Russians have failed to occupy us. So now they are carrying out massive attacks and mass killings. "They want to destroy our bridges... our data centres, the internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to flee their cities."Putin insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea."Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," Putin said after his Thursday's wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum.Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helps the Kremlin finance the war.Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.

schema.headline: Intensified Russian strikes are tearing Kyiv apart, Klitschko warns

title: Alison Hammond has heart check-up in hospital after leaving TV's This Morning
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByPaul GlynnCulture reporterUpdated 1 hour agoAlison Hammond went to hospital for a heart check-up after leaving ITV's This
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByPaul GlynnCulture reporterUpdated 1 hour agoAlison Hammond went to hospital for a heart check-up after leaving ITV's This Morning midway through Friday's show, but has assured followers she is "fine".The presenter, 51, left the programme during its live broadcast, appearing to clutch her chest as she was assisted off the set by co-host Dermot O'Leary. He later told viewers she was "feeling a little unwell".In a video posted from a hospital bed, external on Friday afternoon, Hammond said she had "a little bit of a palpitation" during the show but was feeling OK and was undergoing tests."I know you're all worried about me," she said. "Honestly, I am fine. First of all, I'm getting my old ticker checked out."Image source, Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockImage caption, Hammond and O'Leary were presenting Friday's edition of This MorningShe continued: "I had a little bit of a palpitation, and now I'm getting it all checked out. But I think I'm OK. I'm hoping it was just a little panic attack or something like that."The Birmingham-born presenter, who also co-hosts The Great British Bake Off, thanked This Morning's viewers for sending her "lovely messages" while apologising for her dramatic early exit."I'm so sorry I left you," she added. "I would never normally do that. I would never leave a TV show, so you know I wasn't very well."But hopefully I'm going to be all right. The doctors are so lovely, and they're checking me out, and hopefully everything's going to be fine."Everything is fine, look. I'm rocking it. Look how good I look," she joked, noting how she was still wearing her make-up from the show.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, O'Leary and Hammond are the regular This Morning presenting partnership on FridaysFriday's edition of the ITV show began at 10:00 BST with Hammond and her regular co-host O'Leary at the helm, before she left at 11:30 during a segment about pets.O'Leary, 53, addressed her absence when the show returned from a break, saying: "Welcome back to This Morning, Alison is feeling a little unwell, so she's just had to duck out. Hopefully she'll be back."He later updated viewers that she would, in fact, not be returning, "so I'll be here for the rest of the show".Hammond initially rose to fame as contestant on Channel 4 reality show Big Brother before appearing on I'm A Celebrity and Strictly Come Dancing.She became a co-host in This Morning in 2021, and was part of the team that won a National Television Award for best daytime programme the following year.She joined Bake Off in 2023 and took over from the late Paul O'Grady on For the Love of Dogs in 2024.

schema.headline: Alison Hammond has heart check-up in hospital after leaving TV's This Morning

title: Olivia Dean accused of copying Bill Withers' Just The Two of Us
description: British pop star Olivia Dean has been accused of copying the melody of Bill Withers' soul classic Just The Two of Us in a legal case filed in Californ
body: British pop star Olivia Dean has been accused of copying the melody of Bill Withers' soul classic Just The Two of Us in a legal case filed in California.The complaint centres around Dean's song I've Seen It, taken from her Brit Award-winning 2025 album The Art of Loving.Just The Two of Us was a hit for Withers in 1981, and the publishers of the late singer's catalogue allege that the two songs "share musical features" that are "so striking" they cannot have arisen by coincidence alone.The lawsuit names Dean's record label Capitol Records, parent company Universal Music Group and her publishing companies as the defendants. It does not seek damages from the singer herself or her co-writers Bastian Langebæk and Max Wolfgang.In legal documents seen by the BBC, Mattie Music Group, which looks after Withers' back catalogue, said it hired a musicologist to review the two songs.He concluded "that the works contain substantial similarities" including the "repeated copying" of the melody from Just The Two of Us, the documents said.The publishers claim they notified Dean's record label of the potential infringement in August, but the music was not pulled from distribution.To prove plagiarism, Mattie Music Group would have to prove that Dean and her co-writers had previously heard Withers' original composition.In the lawsuit, they allege that his song's "extraordinary and sustained" commercial success, including "decades of radio play", would mean the musicians had "reasonable opportunity" to have encountered Just The Two of Us before writing I've Seen It.The defendants have yet to respond to the lawsuit. The BBC has contacted them, and Dean's representatives, for a comment.I've Seen It is the closing track of Dean's breakthrough album, which was released in September 2025.A sweet, acoustic ballad, it discusses the various types of love she's encountered in her life - from high school crushes to the love she has for her family and friends.Speaking to W Magazine last year, she said the song was written after "I'd had a lot of red wine". "When I heard it back for the first time, I burst into tears. It felt like the loveliest note to end on. Whether it's within your friends, your family, or just the love that exists in the strangers around you, it's there, and it's inside of you, too."It is has been streamed on Spotify about 246 million times, while Just The Two of Us has racked up 948 million plays.Withers' track went to number two in the US charts in 1981 and earned him a Grammy for best R&B song. He died in 2020.Dean picked up best new artist at this year's Grammys, while The Art of Loving reached number three in the US and number one in the UK, and was named album of the year at the Brit Awards.

schema.headline: Olivia Dean accused of copying Bill Withers' Just The Two of Us

title: Three reasons Middle East oil is nearly back to pre-Iran war levels
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByThomas Copeland and Becky DaleBBC VerifyThe volume of oil flowing from the Middle East region has almost returned to pre-w
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByThomas Copeland and Becky DaleBBC VerifyThe volume of oil flowing from the Middle East region has almost returned to pre-war levels, data shows, despite the continued restrictions Iran is placing on vessels attempting to travel through the Strait of Hormuz.Seven months after the US-Israel war with Iran led to the effective closure of the critical waterway, the maritime intelligence firm Kpler said that in the final week of September, daily oil flow from the Middle East reached 92% of its pre-war baseline.Analysts attribute the rebounding flow of oil to three key factors:Ships being escorted with US military assistanceUsing shuttle tankers through the strait for transfer to different vesselsBypassing the strait using pipelinesBut some experts have questioned the sustainability of these measures, given the risk of escalating Iranian attacks or a change in US policy.About 40% of the total oil exported from the region in September bypassed the strait and exited via overland pipelines to ports on the Red Sea or the Gulf of Oman, up from 17% before the war, according to Kpler.Oil exports from Iran, however, have ground to a halt after the reimposition of a US naval blockade in July.US military assistanceThe US military has been supporting ships as they pass through the Strait of Hormuz since at least mid-June and US Navy data shows the number of vessels assisted by US forces is up by a third in September compared with August.Martin Kelly, senior intelligence analyst at security firm EOS Risk Group, told BBC Verify that US support is primarily in the form of "air support to ships", including through issuing warnings and intercepting incoming threats from drones, missiles or boats.But ships moving through the US-recommended southern route of the strait near the coast of Oman, rather than seeking permission to use Iran's northern route, continue to be targeted.September saw the highest number of successful Iranian attacks on commercial shipping since March, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data conflict monitor.Naveen Das, a senior oil analyst from Kpler, said the market oil market "doesn't trust that we're going stay in this status quo" because of the risk of further Iranian escalation and the possible impact of the US midterm elections.Ship-to-ship transfersMost of the oil passing through the strait now moves via a "shuttle system" of more than 60 large oil tankers moving back and forth, according to Kpler.More than 70% of the crude oil which passed through the strait in August was transferred from these "shuttle tankers" onto other vessels in the Gulf of Oman, Kpler said.BBC Verify has analysed satellite imagery which appears to show these ship-to-ship transfers, seemingly more protected from Iranian attack, taking place off the coast of the Omani port city, Sohar.But there is a "question over how long these ships can last", said Martin Kelly, particularly as attacks on them continue.Imagery taken on 24 September shows six pairs of ships docked or paired together near the port.An average of more than four million barrels of oil per day was transferred from ship to ship in the Gulf of Oman over in the week to 30 September, according to Kpler.Overall, an average of 12 million barrels of oil per day passed through the strait over this period, compared with a pre-war baseline of 17 million.PipelinesOil exporting countries in the Gulf have also responded to Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz by exporting more crude oil overland via pipelines.Just under 20% of crude is now leaving the region from ports on the Red Sea at the end of Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, which is recording exports of more than four million barrels per day, according to Kpler.Three weeks after an attack on this pipeline blamed on Iran-backed proxies in Iraq, Saudi Arabia is now exporting through the pipeline at "full stretch", according to Kpler.Almost a quarter of all crude flowing from the region is now being piped past the Strait of Hormuz to terminals along the Gulf of Oman, particularly the city of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Kpler's data shows.Naveen Das from Kpler said this increased use of pipelines is likely to become the "new normal" because "it seems very improbable that we live in a world whereby the Gulf countries and Iran go back to being relatively harmonious".Oil exports from Iran have fallen almost to zero following the re-imposition of a US blockade in mid-July, down from 1.7 million barrels a day before the war began, Kpler data shows.There are 20 empty Iran-flagged tankers currently off the coast of Sri Lanka, unable to return to the Gulf due to the US blockade, according to ship-tracking data and analysis from the US-based advocacy and monitoring organisation United Against Nuclear Iran.While crude oil flow from the Middle East has resumed to almost normal levels, exports of liquified natural gas and oil products like jet fuel and have remained well below pre-conflict volumes.Fewer than a million barrels of processed oil products passed through the Strait of Hormuz on average in the last week, down from 3.5 million per day before the war began.Additional reporting by Rob England and Richard Irvine-Brown, graphics by Tom Shiel

schema.headline: Three reasons Middle East oil is nearly back to pre-Iran war levels

title: 'Ashamed': Cornell students gather to voice anger over alleged gang rape
description: Figure caption, Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape caseByNada TawfikNew York correspondent at Cornell University and Saksh
body: Figure caption, Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape caseByNada TawfikNew York correspondent at Cornell University and Sakshi VenkatramanStudents have called for drastic change at Cornell University as a result of an alleged gang rape in 2024, with one using an emotional student assembly on Thursday to say: "We're absolutely ashamed of the events that happened on campus."Students and faculty members say the investigation into the incident has cast a "dark cloud" over the campus - stirring anger, concern over fraternity culture, and a backlash against the university's handling of the situation.At Thursday's assembly, some labelled the perceived lack of justice a "disgrace" and criticised the prestigious university, which has defended its handling of the case."We deserve to know that our institution values our safety more than its reputation," undergraduate Sophia Riley Sim told those at the gathering.Sim said she had been too upset by the case to attend classes for the past week.Under normal circumstances, the Ivy League university is a beautiful place to study at this time of year. Autumn leaves bring pops of colour to its stately buildings, which are set against the backdrop of the rolling hills of upstate New York.But students and staff who spoke to the BBC - some on condition of anonymity - said the tension on campus had become palpable since the 2024 case resurfaced in recent weeks.Image source, Lauren Petracca / ReutersImage caption, Cornell University's campus is located in Ithaca, upstate New YorkThe accuser at the centre of the alleged gang rape, known anonymously as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell on 16 September, saying she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house during the incident two years ago.She claimed that Cornell had failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved in the incident. The men have been dubbed the Cornell Seven.Cornell has already agreed to an independent investigation into the rape allegation. The university has also defended its handling of the issue to date, external, saying it conducted an "extensive investigation" that lasted several months following the report of the incident, and that it followed applicable federal civil rights law.Shortly after Thursday's student assembly at Cornell, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced she had appointed the state attorney general, Letitia James, as special prosecutor in the case. She said she had "lost faith" in the Tompkins County district attorney, who was previously leading the investigation. James therefore takes over the case from Matthew Van Houten. Van Houten's office initially concluded that the evidence did not meet the legal threshold to bring charges - before reopening a criminal investigation last week in light of the new civil complaint, a move that Cornell supported.An upcoming "Justice for Survivors" protest, planned at the university for 5 October, is being advertised in flyers all over campus. It calls on Cornell to take action against alleged rape culture.Student organisers are calling for Cornell to expel and revoke the degrees of the alleged perpetrators of the rape, rewrite policies around sexual assault punishments, initiate an external investigation of the university and mandate prevention training for campus police.As part of its account of its prior investigation of the case, Cornell says: "At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell."Cornell says it is legally prevented from publicly disclosing specific disciplinary outcomes about disciplinary students, adding that "we recognise that this legal limitation can be frustrating".Across campus, the case has stirred anger.One fourth-year student recalled that it had been hard to live there in 2024, in the aftermath of the incident, as rumours began spreading about Jane Doe.Now, two years on, she told the BBC how she and her friends felt "overwhelmed" and "disappointed", comparing the atmosphere on campus to a "dark cloud". Cornell, she believes, mishandled things.She wants the administration to admit what she sees as its mistakes, calling the lack of transparency disheartening.She also asked why multiple men in a group chat for members of Chi Phi - the fraternity group at the centre of the allegations - did not speak up. A chapter of the fraternity was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.Image source, Lauren Petracca / ReutersImage caption, Students and staff have spoken of a "dark cloud" over the campusStudents and community members also used Thursday's student assembly meeting to vent their frustrations and disappointment."I am very disgusted to be here, to be paying this institution to be here," freshman Eliana Dolven-Miller said. "There was a lot of anger in that room, I was very angry."Eeshaan Chaudhuri, the student assembly chair, opened the meeting by saying that the campus stood "with victims of sexual violence"."We don't tolerate it here on campus, and I think I can speak for every single one of us, and I can say we're absolutely ashamed of the events that happened on our campus," Chaudhuri said.The student group has also raised a resolution calling on the university to release a written account of how it handled the alleged sexual assault, including what evidence was gathered and whether and when the university referred the matter to campus police.Figure caption, "I'm very shocked" - College students react to Cornell University rape investigationA faculty member said the mood on campus was "dismal". Staff were not trained therapists, she said, so it was hard to know how to navigate these discussions with students.It was an "incredible situation that was so… I just don't understand," she said, adding that she was unsure if the university should have gone further, and adding that this was not the first time a fraternity group had had problems on campus.Some of the freshmen, or first-year students, who spoke to the BBC had only arrived at Cornell last month.A young woman said she and her friends had been discussing the allegations again that morning. Her friend said it had been difficult for him to come to an Ivy League university feeling excited about the future, only to see this story dominate the news.Students were not OK about what happened to Jane Doe, he said.Cornell alumni have also given their views.More than 1,300 graduates have signed a letter calling on the university to take "swift and expansive" action after the allegations came back to light."Will Cornell take this as an opportunity to ask difficult questions about the proliferation of sexual violence on its own campus?" asks the letter, which was published in the university's student newspaper."Or will it shy away from reform to protect its image? This is not an isolated incident."

schema.headline: 'Ashamed': Cornell students gather to voice anger over alleged gang rape

title: Dolly Parton sings Jolene in Welsh in recording released after her death
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dolly's niece Jada Star and Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis say the country singer was "proud" to sing
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dolly's niece Jada Star and Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis say the country singer was "proud" to sing in WelshByEllie Carter and Miriam BarkerBBC WalesA new version of Dolly Parton's Jolene is set to be released, with parts of the song sung in Welsh by the legendary country artist.The song was recorded before her death on 25 August, and is a collaboration with Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis as well as Parton's niece, Jada Star.In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote more than 3,000 songs.The single will come out on 9 October, and is the second posthumous release from Parton - who was of Welsh descent.In a teaser video released on social media, Star and Lewis explained how the song came to light.As a proud Welsh speaker, Lewis, from Neath, had started translating some of her favourite tunes, and soon landed on the Parton classic, Jolene."Two years ago I posted a video of me singing the Dolly Parton classic Jolene in Welsh, external," said Lewis."I never expected it would go viral and definitely didn't expect it to attract the attention of Dolly's family - especially her niece Jada."Image source, Bronwen LewisImage caption, Dolly Parton's niece, Jada, got in touch with Bronwen Lewis after hearing her sing Jolene in WelshA friendship was born, and Star came over from Nashville in the US to Wales to meet Lewis, joining her at Pride Cymru."Pride Cymru was such an amazing experience and I learned so much about my family lineage," said Star."I cherish the time I spent with Bronwen exploring one of the most beautiful places I have ever seen."Image source, Bronwen LewisImage caption, Jada Star asked her aunt, Dolly Parton, if she would sing with her and Bronwen on a version of JoleneThe teaser revealed it was Star's suggestion to record Jolene in Welsh, which Lewis "jumped" at the chance to do, with Star then saying she would get her aunt involved too."Jada told me that her Aunt Dolly would like to sing with us on our version of Jolene. I think I fell to the ground," said Lewis."Definitely cried happy tears, and called my mother immediately."BBC Radio Wales presenter Lewis said she had always loved Parton's music."To hear Dolly sing in another language, and in Welsh for the very first time, was unbelievable."Figure caption, Watch: 'Where's Jolene now? You can have him, Jolene'After understanding the phonetics of Lewis' translation, Parton recorded her parts at her studio in Nashville, in early 2025. Lewis had planned to go over to meet her to release the music, but Parton passed away before the meet-up could happen."It was devastating, not just for myself and our family, but for the entire world," Star said.Lewis said the pair realised what a privilege it was to have recorded and collaborated "with one of the greatest musicians and women to grace this Earth"."We did what she always told us to do. We got ourselves together and decided to finish what we started," Star added.Star and Lewis said Parton was "proud" to sing in Welsh.This is not the first time Parton has featured on songs in another language.She has appeared on several Latin songs and also collaborated on a track with an Irish folk band in 2011.Before her death, Parton revealed she had recorded a song with U2 which is set to be released in November. She also teased fans about a track which has been kept in a time capsule until its planned release in 2046.Image source, Bronwen LewisImage caption, Bronwen and Jada recorded Jolene in the UK, while Dolly recorded her parts at her studio in NashvilleIn 2008, during a concert at the Cardiff International Arena, Parton reportedly revealed her Welsh ancestry to fans in the crowd."Some of my mother's people, the Owens, are from there [Wales]," Parton later told Wales Online."I've been there about three times and it always feels good because it feels like family."Star had also previously spoken about the family's Welsh connection.She said the Owens side of the family, coming from Parton's mother Avie Lee Owens, was believed to have come from Conwy.Speaking to BBC Radio Wales in 2024, Star said discovering that part of the family's history had been "really extraordinary".Star suggested some of Parton's music, and her own, may have been inspired by her Welsh roots.Parton's death brought renewed attention in Wales to the country music legend's Welsh links, with her heritage explored in a 2025 documentary.Following the singer's death, research by staff at Conwy council's archives suggested Parton's ancestors were from Machynlleth, not Conwy as previously thought.

schema.headline: Dolly Parton sings Jolene in Welsh in recording released after her death

title: I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's
description: It's not uncommon for lethal injections - the most frequently used form of capital punishment in the 27 US states where the penalty is legal - to be "
body: It's not uncommon for lethal injections - the most frequently used form of capital punishment in the 27 US states where the penalty is legal - to be "botched". The Death Penalty Information Center, a think-tank that does not take a stance on the death penalty, describes a botched execution as one with "unanticipated problems or delays that caused, at least arguably, unnecessary agony for the prisoner or that reflect gross incompetence of the executioner". The organisation has compiled a list of 64 botched executions since 1982, 51 of them lethal injections. In at least seven of those cases, the executions were halted because the IV line could not be set.But Graczyk has never seen an execution fail after the injection was delivered."That has never happened here," Graczyk said of the Lone Star State.Graczyk, who covered a wide range of topics for the AP during his 46 years with the news service, considers his prolific attendance at executions to be an important part of the job."There is no [greater] authority, power, or whatever you want to call it, that state or federal government has over us than the power to take our life," he said.There have been 1,683 executions in the US since 1976,  according to the Death Penalty Information Centre, which is when the US Supreme Court re-instated the death penalty. Texas has carried out by far the most of any state, with 602 executions. In 1982, it became the first state to use lethal injections to execute people. Why the death penalty is on the rise in US"I always thought it was important for someone who has no stake in the outcome of a case to be there and to see the law being carried out and to make certain that it is done properly," Graczyk said."That someone is there to see it and tell others: Here's what I saw. Here's what happened."Although he is technically retired, he still works freelance for AP covering executions in his home state.He feels a particular responsibility to remember victims in his coverage and it's especially disheartening when he writes a story about an execution that doesn't make big news. "I feel bad for the victims in the case," he said. "They are the forgotten folks. They always have been.""Today, all the emphasis is on the inmate in Tennessee," he said. "No tears are being shed, other than the victim's immediate family, for the victim … and I understand that's the business we're in, but it doesn't mean it's right."Pike's victim was Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old originally from Florida who loved to roller skate, smile and help others, according to descriptions given by her friends and family. Slemmer was tortured and killed by Pike, then 18, and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, after they met her at a job training camp.Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was present in Tennessee on Wednesday for the execution attempt, telling NBC News afterwards that it "was a mess".Texas, where Graczyk lives and works, does not allow observers in the execution chamber when the IV is being inserted, he said."So when we get into the chamber, the inmate's already hooked up."In a lethal injection execution, the IV would typically be inserted in the crook of the person's arm, Graczyk said. But if that didn't work, sometimes it would go into the top of their hand, their leg, neck or other sites.During successful executions, Graczyk said inmates become "visibly unconscious after just a few seconds". They are usually pronounced dead 20 to 40 minutes after the fatal dose is given, he said.He still remembers the death of Jonathan Nobles, who was executed by lethal injection in Texas in 1998. He'd been handed the sentence after his conviction for the brutal 1986 stabbing murders of two Austin women, Kelley Fraquhar and Mitzi Johnson-Nalley.Nobles sang "Silent Night" as his last words."He gets to 'Round yon virgin' and he stops talking," Graczyk told BBC News. "That's how long it took for the drug to kick in so he wasn't conscious anymore."That scene has stuck with Graczyk for nearly 30 years."To this day, when I'm in church on Christmas, and the choir is singing Silent Night, and all the congregation is joining in Silent Night and they're all, you know, in the spirit of the season and the joy of the season, and I'm thinking of this execution, I'm sure I'm the only one in that congregation that is having that kind of recollection."When people hear about his career covering executions, he said, they are usually curious."Most people don't get to watch someone die," he said.But when people ask him about what he has witnessed, he tells them "it's not the only thing I did or do or have done".

schema.headline: I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's

title: K-pop giants Stray Kids join BTS in boycotting the 2027 Grammy Awards
description: One of the world's biggest K-pop groups, Stray Kids, are joining BTS in boycotting the 2027 Grammy Awards.The move comes after the introduction of a c
body: One of the world's biggest K-pop groups, Stray Kids, are joining BTS in boycotting the 2027 Grammy Awards.The move comes after the introduction of a controversial new category for Asian pop music, which critics fear will ghettoise genres like K-Pop and J-Pop.BTS announced they would not submit songs for consideration in any category in July, saying they hoped their music "can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language".Stray Kids, who recently scored their ninth US number one album, have now followed suit. In a short statement, their record label JYP simply said: "Stray Kids did not submit for the Grammys."Stray Kids had previously refrained from giving a direct answer to questions about the awards.During a press conference for their latest album, This and That, in August, singer Hwang Hyun-jin said: "We have never once set award results or records as our goal."Our top priority is for our fans to be happy and satisfied," he added.The news will come as a blow to the Recording Academy, which organises the Grammys. Stray Kids are phenomenally popular in the US, and recently headlined the Governor's Ball festival in New York, sharing the bill with Lorde and A$AP Rocky. In the album chart, only one other band has scored more number one albums: The Beatles.Earlier this year, all eight members of the band were given voting privileges at the awards, which gives additional weight to their decision to withdraw. BTS are also voting members of the Academy.The Recording Academy announced the new category in June, saying it would recognise "artistic excellence in Asian pop music performances originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets".The prize had been under discussion for years. It was finally introduced after  Golden, from the movie K-pop Demon Hunters, became the first K-Pop song ever to win a Grammy this February."As Asian pop's influence has continued to grow within our process, our members and trustees felt this was the right moment to create a category that more accurately reflects the genre's scale, artistry and global impact," organisers said at the time.But the award received a decidedly mixed reception. Many felt it would stop Asian artists from receiving recognition in the main categories.Others were upset by a stipulation that nominated songs should make "meaningful use" of an Asian language. That requirement ruled out the two most recognisable Korean acts in America, BTS and Blackpink, whose latest releases are primarily sung in English. The arguments against the Asian pop award are similar to those made by Latin artists about Grammy categories such as best música urbana.While the intent is to recognise music of a certain geographic or linguistic origin,  some musicians feel it ends up being exclusionary, with their music segregated from mainstream prizes like album or song of the year.That perception was challenged this year, when Bad Bunny's Debí Tirar Más Fotos  became the first Spanish-language album to win album of the year. Rosalía's Lux is also expected to feature heavily in the nominations for next year's awards.

schema.headline: K-pop giants Stray Kids join BTS in boycotting the 2027 Grammy Awards

title: What's really going on with the lymphatic drainage beauty trend videos?
description: Image source, Abbey AlexandraImage caption, Abbey Alexandra performs lymphatic drainage massages a couple of times a weekByEmily HoltUpdated 5 hours a
body: Image source, Abbey AlexandraImage caption, Abbey Alexandra performs lymphatic drainage massages a couple of times a weekByEmily HoltUpdated 5 hours agoIf she's ever feeling bloated, Abbey Alexandra has a go-to routine, using body oil and a wooden roller to perform stomach massages.The 31-year-old from Birmingham shares before-and-after videos on TikTok, saying she feels the process leaves her depuffed and defined: "You definitely feel a lot better after, they are relaxing."The technique is a form of lymphatic drainage massage, adapted from a medical treatment and shared as a beauty trend. Celebrity fans include Maya Jama, who shares her clinic sessions, and actress Hailey Bieber, who told Time magazine: "I swear by them."Whether there is a physical change - or any need for one - is debatable, but fans of the massages claim they help "flatten" and "debloat" and give a "snatched waist" and "sculpted abs". But what's actually happening to their bodies?What do the videos show?Image source, Abbey AlexandraImage caption, Before-and-after video grabs of a form of lymphatic drainage massage Many videos on social media promoting lymphatic massage show a woman either standing sideways, facing the front or perhaps lying down with her stomach showing a slight - and very normal - curve outwards.Then begins the methodical massage in circular motions seemingly draining fluid away. By the end, her stomach appears flatter - if a little red.But social media body trends should always be viewed with scepticism, says Dr Ella Guest, senior research fellow and health psychologist at the Centre for Appearance Research based at the University of the West of England."These images might be altered using photo-editing tools or filters, people standing in particular poses, use of lighting, lots could even be AI-generated," she says."I think stopping to reflect on what you see and questioning whether it looks realistic, or if it's very aligned with beauty standards, can be useful. Remember, if something looks too good to be true, it probably is."What is the lymphatic system? The lymphatic system is a network of channels and glands throughout the body that helps fight infection and remove excess fluid, according to the NHS.Dr Xand van Tulleken tells Morning Live that the lymphatic system helps remove excess fluid from tissues and supports the immune system."When it is not working properly, it can contribute to swelling, which can be a condition called lymphoedema."This commonly affects people who have cancers that involve the lymph system or who've had treatment involving the lymph nodes.It causes swelling in any part of the body, but usually develops in the arms or legs."In simple terms, the lymphatic system helps keep your body's fluid levels balanced, cleans up waste, and supports your defences against illness," says van Tulleken.Draining your lymphatic systemDr Xand explains how to drain your lymphatic system.What's the massage doing?Image source, Abbey AlexandraImage caption, Abbey says lymphatic drainage massage makes her feel less bloatedDr Xand says manual lymphatic drainage is one of a range of treatments used by medical professionals "if your lymphatic system isn't working as it should". He describes it as using "light pressure" and "strategic massage techniques" to "clear" your lymphatic system. "They'll coax excess lymph fluid from your swollen tissues toward your lymph nodes, where the lymph can reabsorb," he says - adding lymph nodes are found in the armpits, neck and groin. He adds that these massages can be a "safe way" to relieve symptoms for conditions like lymphoedema but are not suitable for some people with pre-existing medical conditions. He stresses: "No one should get their health advice from Instagram - far safer to use the NHS website, or consult your GP."Abbey, who has endometriosis which she says causes her to feel bloated, began doing her own massage routines twice a week aer seeing social media posts about lymphatic drainage."I started using my hands and then I bought some wooden tools as well."After doing my routine, I personally feel less puffy and bloated, particularly around my stomach."Visually, I notice that my stomach looks a little more defined and I also feel lighter and more comfortable."Does it work?Figure caption, Draining your lymphatic systemDr Xand says there is "no need" for most people to perform lymphatic drainage treatments at home."There is very little high-quality evidence showing they provide meaningful or lasting benefits for healthy individuals, and it does not promote fat loss," he says.But he does note that lymphatic drainage massages can feel "relaxing" and some people "can notice a temporary reduction in swelling"."For most healthy people, regular movement, exercise and staying hydrated are all that's needed to support normal lymphatic function," he says."Unless someone has a diagnosed lymphatic condition, I don't think anyone needs routine lymphatic drainage treatments, despite the growing popularity of these practices on social media."For Abbey, it's something she enjoys. "I know the visual difference is temporary... But I do like how I look and feel afterwards so it'll always be a part of my routine."However, Guest warns striving for a sculpted stomach could "feed into people's insecurities"."We know that when we compare ourselves online and try to live up to these trends, we tend to scrutinise our appearance more and feel less satisfied with how we look," she says."The reality is that healthy bodies come in a wide range of shapes and sizes."

schema.headline: What's really going on with the lymphatic drainage beauty trend videos?

title: Anthony Gordon: How Barcelona winger became one of England's main men
description: Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Declan Rice, Jordan Pickford and now Anthony Gordon.All have become guaranteed starters and reliable stars for England, w
body: Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Declan Rice, Jordan Pickford and now Anthony Gordon.All have become guaranteed starters and reliable stars for England, with the Barcelona winger the latest to look, according to captain Kane, like one of the Three Lions' "main men".Gordon was one of England's standout players at the World Cup and earned a big-money move to European giants Barca in the summer, while his good form has continued into his country's Nations League campaign. He scored the opening goal in England's 2-0 win against the Czech Republic on Tuesday night, after also netting in a 3-2 defeat by world champions Spain at Wembley on Saturday.In fact, the 25-year-old's England form has been building since the knockout stage of the World Cup began - his run of averaging a goal contribution every 69 minutes started with assisting both Kane's efforts in a 2-1 last-32 victory over DR Congo.The former Newcastle player has scored three goals and provided three assists in his past six England matches, while he also won the penalty in England's dramatic last-16 victory over Mexico at Azteca Stadium.And after a positive start in Spain, where he has already picked up five assists in La Liga, Gordon looks to be joining boss Thomas Tuchel's  "undroppable" bracket.Tuchel likes to give his players clarity on their role and makes clear who they are up against in the squad and for a starting position.When asked whether Gordon is getting to be one of the first names on the team-sheet, he said: "He's getting there. He's defending his shirt, he's defending his position - an excellent performance again after his performance against Spain."He was very decisive [against the Czech Republic] and had an excellent goal. It was very, very difficult but the technique and finishing was excellent."He scored against Spain so he has decisive actions and he's defending his shirt and his position. He does it on the highest level and he's a very important player."Gordon linked up well with his former Newcastle team-mate Lewis Hall on England's left and combined with right-back Trent Alexander-Arnold, who was making his first start for the Three Lions in nearly two years, for the opening goal.Gordon said he had been "dying" to link up with Alexander-Arnold, who is also playing in Spain for Barcelona's rivals Real Madrid."It's a great compliment and it's great to play with him," Alexander-Arnold said of Gordon."I tried to get the ball, and try and see what the best play is and try and play forward and create something. And I was able to get the pass."Captain and record goalscorer Kane is a guaranteed starter in England's biggest matches but the position to the left of Kane has been a problem area for the team, with no player able to make it their own. Gordon looks to have secured that role and Kane said the winger is "showing that he belongs at the highest level, for Barcelona and England"."His performances in the last couple of games have been some of his best that he has played in an England shirt," Kane said."I think he is just relishing putting the shirt on and being one of the main men in the team. He is an important player for us and he showed that during the World Cup."It has not always been a straightforward route into the team for Gordon.Marcus Rashford, Eberechi Eze, Phil Foden and Noni Madueke have all featured for England from the left in the past couple of years.Gordon started to emerge as a clear option during Lee Carsley's time in interim charge, but said himself last October that he had only shown "50%" of what he can do for England.Now that seems to be coming to fruition. Against the Czech Republic he attempted four shots, more than any England player and more than any of his team-mates against Spain too.Gordon is ranked in at least the top four of England players for expected assists (0.9), expected goals (0.9), passes into the box (14), touches in the opposition box (29), chances created (eight), and shots on target (five), since the start of the World Cup knockout stage.His importance is underlined by the fact he has contributed the same amount of goals and assists, six, as Bellingham since England faced DR Congo.There has been an interesting subplot with Gordon and Rashford competing for a left-wing space for England and effectively Barcelona.Rashford was on loan at Barcelona last season but they opted to not make his move permanent, instead he returned to Manchester United while the Catalan club splashed out £69m to sign Gordon from Newcastle.Gordon has the ability to take on his full-back on the inside or beat them for pace on the outside before putting in a cross. "People raised eyebrows when Anthony Gordon went to Barcelona for the money that he did and Marcus Rashford came back to Manchester United," former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson told BBC Radio 5 Live."He has become a key part of the England team. There were certain games in the World Cup where he was substituted and he shouldn't have been - I think others should have come off instead of him."Gordon [when he is] full of confidence running at pace like he does, he can go either way and he's causing full-backs all kind of problems."Gordon says that since his move to Spain he has changed people's perception of him being a player who is only quick and presses well, even if they are two of his best attributes."I always felt in England, people respected me because I was fast and I pressed but they never actually respected the quality and IQ that I play with," Gordon told ITV."Only the players I play with ever seem to notice that. I think now I'm at Barcelona and I play a different style, those qualities are highlighted much more and people are actually starting to take notice that I'm not just quick."In England, it was never really respected because people just see me as really quick and really aggressive."In Spain, they really appreciate my IQ and quality because at Barca, if you're not technical, if you're not smart, you're going to stand out like a sore thumb."Tuchel is starting to build a team he thinks can challenge and win the Euros in 2028.But first he wants to win the Nations League, and if England are to do that, it is likely Gordon will have played a huge part.

schema.headline: Anthony Gordon: How Barcelona winger became one of England's main men
